public_rationale: The research shows adoption, uneven willingness to pay and unsettled pricing strategies. It does not establish that interchangeable competing features caused the difficulty charging premiums. Uncertain usefulness is another explanation identified in the contemporaneous research. Neither product proliferation nor weak demand alone settles the causal claim.
limitations: The available survey summaries lack the comparisons needed to identify causation.
The claim's population, quality standard and excessive-cost threshold are unspecified.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: It feels like hundreds of companies have made AI summaries, generative features and search so commonplace that they are effectively commoditized, so everyone is expected to offer mediocre tools that cost too much to run, making them harder to sell at a premium.

statement.excerpt: Instead, it feels like hundreds of companies have joined a death cult, making AI-powered summaries, generative features and search so commonplace that they're effectively commoditized, making it an unspoken expectation that everyone has to offer mediocre tools that cost too much to run, thereby making it harder to flog them to customers at a premium.

our_interpretation: The checkable core is that widespread availability of comparable SaaS AI features reduced customers' willingness to pay an additional premium by the post date.
Commoditized means sufficiently interchangeable to weaken pricing power. It does not mean every feature was free.
The language about quality and excessive costs supplies no independent numerical threshold. Feature availability, weak demand and high costs alone would not establish the claimed causal connection.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous purchasing or pricing research shows that substitutable AI summaries, generation and search features materially reduced SaaS providers' ability to obtain premiums, with operating-cost evidence supporting the cost component.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable research directly tests the proposed mechanism and finds that widespread substitutable features did not weaken pricing power, or that meaningful differentiation sustained premiums across the relevant market.

evidence.explanation: The survey summary reports widespread use alongside uneven willingness to pay and uncertainty about returns. It supplies alternative explanations for weak premiums and does not isolate commoditization as their cause.
The September survey describes differing monetization strategies. It does not measure whether competing features caused lower realized premiums or whether their operating costs were excessive.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Representative purchasing and provider data from the target period linking changes in premiums to comparable competing features, with matched delivery-cost evidence.
